catalog_quote: Primary stress in Tawbuid is either final or penultimate. Most words are stressed unpredictably, and in some speakers, all syllables seem to be equally stressed. Modification in stress occurs in affective speech (see below). Some syllable patterns have predictable stress. A word containing two adjacent syllables with CVC patterns are stressed on the second of those two syllables, whether final or not. /nabag'bag/ 'attacked with knife' /bulat'lat/ 'species of grass' /fag'lon/ 'second most recently born child' /fan'dagum/ 'charm made of resin' /kafan'donan/ 'night is falling' Words with two identical CVC patterns interrupted by /-ar-/ or /-al-/ are also stressed on the second of those two CVC syllables. /falung'fung/ 'sapling' /balang'bang/ 'thigh' Where the final and penultimate syllables are open, and the vowels are the same, the stress is penultimate. susu 'breast' lele 'tongue' langip…

new_statements.quote: Primary stress in Tawbuid is either final or penultimate. Most words are stressed unpredictably, and in some speakers, all syllables seem to be equally stressed. [...] Some syllable patterns have predictable stress. A word containing two adjacent syllables with CVC patterns are stressed on the second of those two syllables, whether final or not. [...] Where the final and penultimate syllables are open, and the vowels are the same, the stress is penultimate. [...] But when the vowels are different, stress can occur unpredictably. final: /nla'fi/ 'flattened' penultimate: /'lafi/ 'shoulder' [...] A root word can change its stress when affixes are added, because affixes carry their own inherent stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexical within a two-syllable window at the right edge: primary stress falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable and is not generally predictable (near-minimal contrasts like /'lafi/ 'shoulder' vs /nla'fi/ 'flattened', /a'fuy/ 'fire' vs /'kafuy/); partial regularities: the second of two adjacent CVC syllables attracts stress (nabag'bag, fan'dagum), CV.CV words with identical vowels are penultimate (susu, lele); affixes carry inherent stress so affixation shifts stress ('sadi 'one', ma'sadi 'united', fagmasadi'un 'unity').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words of more than three syllables have secondary and even tertiary stress (e.g. /²fagma³balyan¹anun/ 'power', /³fag²kedkesu¹ganun/ 'mutual love'); no placement rule given. (Fleming 2022:18 for Eastern Tawbuid: secondary stress optional, position unrestricted, often realises a root's lexical stress when primary stress is forced onto the final two syllables.)
new_statements.exceptions: Some speakers appear to stress all syllables equally; affective/emotive speech lengthens and can move stress (/na'taw/ 'what?' -> /:na:taw/ with rising-then-low pitch for surprise); optional glottal stop between identical vowels attracts stress to the preceding syllable (/fakafanyu'ʔun/ vs /fakafany'u:n/ 'love'); regional 'accents' (Balani, Lagutay, Anawin) differ in pitch contours.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern citation forms of (affixed) words; affixes have inherent stress so the domain is the morphological word. The published grammar of the sister language Eastern Tawbuid (Fleming 2022, SIL e-Books 79, pp.17-18) independently states the same system: contrastive lexical stress with minimal pairs (/sábi/ 'basket' vs /sabí/ 'to slip off'), 'In production, primary stress can only fall on the ultimate or the penultimate syllable of a prosodic word', one obligatory primary stress per prosodic word, inherently stressed affixes (-ún, bà-).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is explicitly about WESTERN Tawbuid (twb, west2559; Occidental Mindoro: Sablayan/Calintaan; local accents Balani, Lagutay, Anawin named) by the OMF linguist who lived there 1988-2001, but its venue is a 2007 Wikipedia contribution (unpublished analysis), not a refereed or archived publication. The only published grammar in the Batangan/Tawbuid cluster is Fleming 2022 (SIL e-Books 79), which describes EASTERN Tawbuid (bnj, Glottolog east2482; fieldwork in Safa, Pula River, Oriental Mindoro) and reports the same system (lexical/contrastive stress confined to the final two syllables). Fleming 2022 should be catalogued under east2482 (the earlier scan had no source found for east2482), not under west2559. Older literature conflates both as 'Batangan' (Zorc 1974, Blust 1991).

sources.note: Primary stress is either final or penultimate; most words stressed unpredictably (lexical), some speakers seem to stress all syllables equally; sub-regularities: second of two adjacent CVC syllables is stressed; CV.CV with identical vowels -> penultimate; affixes carry inherent stress and can shift stress (sadi 'one' vs fagmasadi'un 'unity'); secondary and tertiary stress in words of more than three syllables; affective lengthening can change stress.
